section_summary: This section documents U.S.-British efforts to restrict Japanese access to petroleum, machinery, strategic minerals, metals, and other supplies through export licensing, freezing controls, and coordination with governments in Asia and Latin America. It includes commercial correspondence on oil-payment arrangements, intelligence on Japanese naval oil storage, reports of Japanese purchasing efforts and suspected smuggling, and investigations of attempts to acquire controlled tools and mercury. The section also contains public correspondence about trade with Japan, internal memoranda, cross-reference and charge sheets, and newspaper clippings concerning Axis strategy and American policy.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of British Embassy letter on Mitsubishi well-drilling machinery
subfiles.about: The writer closes a letter warning of Mitsubishi efforts to obtain well-drilling machinery through third countries.
subfiles.summary: This concluding page says that the subject may fall outside Finletter's responsibilities. A duplicate was supplied so that he could forward a copy to another department if appropriate.

subfiles.title: Mitsubishi inquiry for well-drilling machines through Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: The British Embassy reports indications that Mitsubishi may obtain American well-drilling machinery through Argentina for reexport to Japan.
subfiles.summary: London learned that Mitsubishi in Buenos Aires had obtained National Supply Company estimates for four drilling machines and sent the specifications to its Tokyo Ore Department. The quoted prices, delivery terms, and partial equipment specifications are supplied to help identify the prospective order. The Embassy suspects that Argentina would be only the ostensible destination.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning Mitsubishi drilling machinery
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges reports of Mitsubishi attempts to import drilling machinery through Mexico and Argentina.
subfiles.summary: The matter was discussed with the Department's Central Division and the Administrator of Export Control. Both offices promised vigilance, and the reply notes that National Supply Corporation apparently was not the only bidder.

subfiles.title: Forwarding James M. DeFoor's letter about oil shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: William L. Chenery, Crowell Publishing Company
subfiles.about: Collier's editor forwards a former representative's complaint about an editorial discussing petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Chenery explains that he first sent DeFoor's letter to the Department of the Interior. On W. H. McCrillis's advice, he asks the State Department to supply the necessary information.

subfiles.title: Complaint about Collier's editorial on petroleum shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: DeFoor challenges an editorial's account of the supposed exchange obtained for American petroleum sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: DeFoor reports that the freighter James Lykes carried oil in drums or barrels to Japan and returned with sugar and copra loaded in the Philippines. He argues that this contradicts the editorial's implication that the United States received desired Japanese goods in return. He asks Collier's to correct the passage.

subfiles.title: State Department response to William L. Chenery
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The Department responds to DeFoor's questions about the James Lykes returning from Asia with Philippine rather than Japanese cargo.
subfiles.summary: The Department says it lacks information explaining why the James Lykes brought back Philippine cargo. It suggests that Japan's late-July restrictions on funds and property transactions may have affected the return trade and recommends asking Lykes Brothers Steamship Company directly. DeFoor's original letter is returned.

subfiles.title: British policy for licensing exports to China and the Nil List
subfiles.about: Stopford explains British plans to prevent exports to occupied China from benefiting Japan while continuing assistance to free China.
subfiles.summary: Britain intends to license all exports to China except goods sent through the Burma Road and generally to permit normal trade unless supplies are unavailable, economic-warfare grounds dictate refusal, or goods appear on the attached Nil List. Consignee screening, advice from friendly Shanghai banks, and possible quantitative controls are proposed to reduce leakage to Japan. The annex lists twenty-eight prohibited or restricted categories, while petroleum products are expressly excluded from the arrangement.

subfiles.title: Duplicate British letter and Nil List for China
subfiles.about: This is a duplicate copy of the British policy letter and commodity Nil List concerning exports to China.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate repeats the plan to license exports to China, assist legitimate Chinese interests, and prevent leakage to Japan. It again describes consignee and quantitative controls and reproduces the twenty-eight-item Nil List. Petroleum products remain outside the stated arrangements.

subfiles.title: British export controls on trade with Japan
subfiles.about: Stopford reports that Britain will control Empire exports to Japan through export licenses rather than the financial machinery of the Freezing Order.
subfiles.summary: An approved export transaction would receive the necessary financial licenses more or less automatically. In practice, British Empire trade with Japan would be restricted to specially approved transactions. A copy was also sent to Cochran.

subfiles.title: Duplicate letter on British export controls for Japan
subfiles.about: This duplicate reiterates Britain's decision to use export licensing to control Empire trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The copy states that financial permission would follow an approved export license. It emphasizes that only specially approved transactions would be allowed and notes that Cochran was informed.

subfiles.title: Instruction to forward an enclosure through the Tokyo pouch
subfiles.about: The note directs that an attached instruction be sent through the Tokyo pouch.
subfiles.summary: The instruction is to be forwarded with the pouch closing that day. The decision follows the recommendation in the underlying memorandum.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on secure transmission of instructions to Tokyo
subfiles.about: The memorandum compares existing air-mail arrangements with pouch and courier options for confidential instructions to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Air-mail instructions normally traveled by clipper to Hong Kong and then by open mail to Tokyo. A proposed extension of the Tokyo-Shanghai-Peiping courier service to Manila was under consideration, but implementation could take weeks. Because of the confidential material involved, the memorandum recommends using the Tokyo pouch traveling by American vessel to Shanghai and onward by courier.

subfiles.title: Confidential instruction to Ambassador Grew concerning Chilean iodine
subfiles.about: Hull sends Grew a confidential memorandum about Japan's desire to purchase iodine held by a Chilean corporation.
subfiles.summary: The letter transmits, for Grew's information, a memorandum of Hull's August 18 conversation with the Chilean ambassador. The enclosure itself is not present in this section.

subfiles.title: Netherlands Indies payment procedure for oil delivered to Japan
subfiles.from: G. S. Walden, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Walden confirms a telegram describing a proposed Netherlands Indies payment mechanism for petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Oil companies would state the dollars due, while Japanese buyers would pay the equivalent in guilders in Batavia and exchange control would arrange dollar payment in New York. The procedure was intended to force Japanese buyers to replenish their Netherlands Indies guilder balances through exports before making further purchases. Walden asks for the Department's reaction.

subfiles.title: Mitsui Batavia export-license delay
subfiles.from: G. S. Walden, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Walden forwards a telegram concerning Mitsui's pending Netherlands Indies export-license application and a waiting vessel.
subfiles.summary: Mitsui Batavia reportedly was told that no answer on its license application could be given before August 16. Its ship had remained at the lightship for thirty-six hours, while Van Karnebeek was separately communicating about payment methods. Walden requests advice.

subfiles.title: Cover letter transmitting a Shell petroleum memorandum
subfiles.from: G. S. Walden, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Walden sends Hiss a copy of a memorandum delivered to Shell.
subfiles.summary: Walden says that Shell intended to transmit the enclosed message in code through the British consul. The cover letter supplies the Department with advance information about the communication.

subfiles.title: Enclosed message on Netherlands Indies petroleum-export policy
subfiles.from: Van Karnebeek, Batavia, via The Hague
subfiles.about: The message reports Netherlands Indies deliberations over which petroleum products might be exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Indies government had received technically detailed specifications from the Netherlands minister in Washington that might form the basis for U.S. petroleum exports to Japan. It was deciding which products could be exported from the Indies, but crude oil would not be permitted. Quantities were apparently to be based on 1935-1936 average exports, with the permitted percentage still unknown.

subfiles.title: FBI cover letter transmitting the Hanafusa report
subfiles.about: The FBI transmits a report concerning H. Y. Hanafusa and a possible Neutrality Act violation.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure is Special Agent R. F. Cartwright's August 25 report from Seattle. The Bureau states that additional information will follow.

subfiles.title: FBI report on H. Y. Hanafusa's attempts to purchase tool bits
subfiles.from: R. F. Cartwright, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: The report investigates Hanafusa's repeated efforts to purchase small quantities of high-speed cobalt tool bits in Seattle.
subfiles.summary: Hardware-company employees reported that a Japanese purchaser sought Momax cobalt tool bits from several Seattle firms and was referred onward when the bits were unavailable. Local police, sheriff, and credit records produced no criminal reference, but Hanafusa was known as a member of the Japanese Chamber of Commerce and as a traveler to Japan. Because prohibited articles were reportedly being carried to Japan in travelers' luggage, immigration authorities were to be consulted about future trips.

subfiles.title: Routing note on a document about exports from Malaya
subfiles.about: Hiss forwards a document left by Mr. Hall concerning exports from Malaya to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Acheson had sent Hiss the attached paper, apparently after receiving it from Hall. Hiss asks that it be passed to the official responsible for the subject in the commercial division.

subfiles.title: Exports from Malaya to Japan
subfiles.from: J. S. Dent or British Embassy
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes British restrictions on strategic exports from Malaya to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Tin and rubber were completely prohibited. Manganese was limited to about sixty percent of normal trade, bauxite to normal trade, and iron ore to a quota of 1.9 million tons, with additional reductions under consideration or expected from port limitations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on British Treasury action against Japanese-benefiting transactions
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a Hong Kong telegram about British Treasury efforts to hinder transactions benefiting Japan.
subfiles.summary: The underlying telegram reported that the Treasury was compiling a list of undesirable European consignees. Instructions were being sent through Hall-Patch to British banks operating in China. The original was filed under a different decimal classification.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Standard-Vacuum on petroleum exports and frozen Japanese balances
subfiles.about: Hiss records discussions with Walden about Shell and Standard-Vacuum sales policies for petroleum exports from the Netherlands Indies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Shell proposed refusing further sales until its frozen Japanese balances were liquidated and cash-payment arrangements established, although it might supply permitted products afterward. Acheson regarded that position as a private sales policy and saw no governmental objection to Standard-Vacuum adopting the same terms. Walden clarified that any deliveries would still depend upon Netherlands authorization and asked whether his company could apply for licenses for normal-quota diesel oil.

subfiles.title: Walden letter on frozen balances and proposed diesel shipments
subfiles.from: G. S. Walden, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company
subfiles.about: Walden supplies telegrams on outstanding Japanese payments and proposed petroleum shipments from the Netherlands Indies.
subfiles.summary: The company calculated unpaid and frozen balances for shipments to Japan and instructed Yokohama to seek remittance. Japanese buyers, after failing to obtain crude oil, explored loading diesel oil under the Batavia agreement, including cargoes for tankers waiting near Sumatra and Formosa. Standard-Vacuum applied for the necessary license but withheld loading instructions until payment arrangements could be settled.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Walden's August 21 letter
subfiles.about: Hiss acknowledges Walden's letter reproducing petroleum-related telegrams discussed by telephone.
subfiles.summary: The reply thanks Walden for setting out the texts of the various messages. It adds no substantive policy decision.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on proposed Réunion sugar shipment to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet references a telegram about reported French-Japanese negotiations for sugar shipments from Réunion.
subfiles.summary: The underlying telegram reported negotiations between the French and Japanese governments. It requested an investigation of the proposed shipment and was filed elsewhere in the decimal system.

subfiles.title: Japanese mineral contracts in Bolivia
subfiles.about: The British Embassy reports Japanese contracts for Bolivian antimony, copper, lead, and wolfram and concern that shipments may miss Japanese sailings.
subfiles.summary: Banco Minero listed outstanding Japanese contracts for 1,000 tons of antimony, 650 tons of copper, 525 tons of lead, and 235 tons of wolfram. Railway difficulties might prevent the minerals from reaching Chilean ports before anticipated Japanese sailings ceased after September 15. Japanese purchasers were paying substantially more for antimony than American buyers.

subfiles.title: Yen letters of credit for Japanese mineral purchases in South America
subfiles.about: The letter explains how the U.S. freezing order changed financing for Japanese purchases of South American metals from dollar to yen letters of credit.
subfiles.summary: Before the freeze, mineral sellers used irrevocable dollar credits handled through banks in Chile, Peru, and Bolivia on behalf of the Yokohama Specie Bank, with local-currency payment at guaranteed exchange rates. Afterward, irrevocable yen credits replaced dollar credits while payment still occurred in local currency. The writer argues that this mechanism shows why continued efforts to deny Japan scarce South American minerals remained necessary.

subfiles.title: State Department summary of Japanese oil stocks and consumption
subfiles.about: The memorandum extracts key estimates from a naval attaché report on Japan's oil position.
subfiles.summary: It gives annual Japanese consumption as five million tons of crude oil and one million tons of gasoline. Total stocks are estimated at ten million tons, while naval storage capacity exceeds three million tons.

subfiles.title: Japanese Naval Oil Storage
subfiles.from: H. H. Smith-Hutton, U.S. Naval Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence and designated recipients
subfiles.about: The report estimates Japanese naval petroleum-storage capacity by base and assesses total stocks and annual consumption.
subfiles.summary: After research and consultation with the British naval attaché, Smith-Hutton estimated naval capacity above 3.33 million tons, with especially large facilities at Kure, Tokuyama, Yokosuka, Maizuru, and Sasebo. The report describes surface and underground tanks at major bases and lists additional storage locations throughout Japan and its overseas possessions. It regards roughly ten million tons as a reasonable estimate of total Japanese oil stocks and gives annual consumption near five million tons of crude and 940,000 tons of gasoline.

subfiles.title: Mercury shipments from Chile to Japan
subfiles.about: Reid-Adam lists recent mercury cargoes shipped from Valparaíso to Japanese ports.
subfiles.summary: Five shipments between April 7 and August 18 are identified by vessel, quantity, shipper or consignee, and destination. Although smaller than former Mexican shipments, the Chilean exports were considered relevant to current negotiations.

subfiles.title: Silk King Studios appeal concerning blocked Japanese merchandise
subfiles.about: Rice protests that American small businesses cannot receive prepaid Japanese goods while other countries continue sending oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rice supports the government's general policy but argues that nonmilitary Japanese merchandise already paid for should be released. His firm had deposits tied up in goods held at Japanese ports, while reports indicated continuing Mexican and South American oil shipments to Japan. He asks that affected American businesses receive consideration during forthcoming discussions with Japanese representatives.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Harold R. Rice
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Rice's concerns about U.S.-Japanese relations and the difficulties facing American firms trading with the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Rice's views and expression of support are acknowledged with appreciation. The Department says it is closely considering the problems of American firms and possible practical assistance and protection for their interests. Page 210 contains only residual filing marks.

subfiles.title: Mitsui purchase order for Argentine wool
subfiles.about: A confidential source reports that Mitsui's Buenos Aires branch was instructed to buy 4.5 million pounds of Argentine wool.
subfiles.summary: The first shipment was to move during the first half of November with cargo space supplied. Efforts to confirm the report in the Boston wool market had neither proved nor disproved it.

subfiles.title: Mitsubishi effort to buy Tarapacá potassium chloride
subfiles.about: The British Embassy reports Mitsubishi efforts to obtain 1,000 tons of Chilean potassium chloride through Buenos Aires.
subfiles.summary: Mitsubishi learned that Chile had informally asked producers to reserve future output for South America and therefore proposed purchasing through its Buenos Aires branch for shipment to China or Japan. The British ambassador at Santiago was instructed to encourage safeguards against reexport. The intelligence source was described as exceptionally sensitive.

subfiles.title: Gerald Fennell's appeal for an embargo on Japanese silk
subfiles.about: Fennell urges a complete embargo on Japanese silk to deny Japan American currency.
subfiles.summary: He argues that continued silk imports provide Japan with more than one hundred million dollars annually that might later finance war against the United States. Because rayon and other synthetics were available and silk was a nonessential luxury, he presents an embargo as consistent with national-defense austerity.

subfiles.title: Undated Gerald Fennell letter fragment on peace advocates
subfiles.about: Fennell comments on an unidentified financial promoter, Mexican interests, and proposed peace emissaries.
subfiles.summary: The fragment mentions losses suffered by English and French investors and the subject's later dealings in Mexican products. Fennell questions his suitability as a peace intermediary between Britain and Germany and refers to the peace advocacy of Senator Wheeler and apparently Verne Marshall. Much of the text is damaged or ambiguous.

subfiles.title: The U.S.A. and the Triple Axis
subfiles.about: Lippmann analyzes Axis military pressure intended to deter effective American support for Britain.
subfiles.summary: The article links Japanese moves toward Singapore with German pressure on Spain, Portugal, Ireland, and Atlantic island bases after the Tripartite Pact. Lippmann argues that the Axis wished to threaten the United States without forcing it fully into the war, because combined British-American sea power and American industrial capacity would be formidable. Pages 216 and 218 contain overlapping or fragmentary clipping text, while page 217 is blank.

subfiles.title: Published letter urging a U.S. declaration of war
subfiles.about: McAllister argues that the United States should declare war directly rather than rely on aid to Britain.
subfiles.summary: He contends that geography, not British resistance, had chiefly prevented Hitler from invading England and predicts efforts to devise invasion craft. McAllister urges Congress to declare war, asserting that American production and military capacity could defeat Hitler more quickly and economically through direct action.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Gerald Fennell
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Fennell's letter to the president advocating an embargo on Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: The letter states that Fennell's views have been carefully noted. It also expresses appreciation for the spirit in which he brought them to the government's attention.

subfiles.title: Reply to Marvin R. Schafer on exports to Japan and policy toward the Soviet Union
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Acting Chief, Division of Exports and Defense Aid
subfiles.about: The Department answers Schafer's questions about war-material exports to Japan and U.S. assistance to the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Allen encloses Export Control Schedule No. 3 and related proclamations, orders, regulations, and press releases to explain controls on strategic exports. He emphasizes that licenses were considered in light of immediate and long-term national-defense consequences. On Soviet policy, the response cites Sumner Welles's June 23 statement and distinguishes aid to forces opposing Hitler from approval of the Soviet regime.

subfiles.title: Marvin R. Schafer's questions on Japan and Soviet policy
subfiles.about: Schafer asks for an administration explanation of continued exports to Japan and support for the Soviet Union after Germany's invasion.
subfiles.summary: He questions reports that steel, gasoline, and other materials were still leaving Puget Sound ports for Japan despite Japanese aggression in China and alliance with Germany. He also asks why German aggression altered U.S. treatment of Stalin's government and communist subversion. Schafer seeks an answer for use in the public discussion groups he leads.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Noel Hall on prospective British trade restrictions
subfiles.about: Hall outlines British thinking on embargoes and strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Britain expected to be conservative about embargoing foodstuffs but was studying iron ore, lead, zinc, bauxite, manganese, salt, mica, fluorspar, and New Guinea copra. Hall also emphasized British interest in bunker control in the Pacific. The meeting continued a conversation begun on July 16.

subfiles.title: Conversation on coordination of U.S. and British measures against Japan
subfiles.about: Acheson and Hornbeck brief Hall on planned U.S. action toward Japan and seek details of corresponding British measures.
subfiles.summary: Hall said Britain expected to denounce some commercial treaties, tighten export and import controls, and urge the Dutch to align with it, but he could not clarify policy on freezing. He noted that direct United Kingdom trade with Japan was small while colonial and dominion trade remained significant. Hornbeck concluded that British plans were vague and limited and that Britain chiefly wished to learn what Washington intended.

subfiles.title: South African embargo on fluorspar exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The British Embassy reports that South Africa is withholding licenses for fluorspar and other important exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The information came from the British Ministry of Economic Warfare. The Union of South Africa was said to be denying export licenses for fluorspar as part of a broader restriction on important commodities.

subfiles.title: Argentine fluorspar exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Reid-Adam reviews Argentine fluorspar production and exports and evaluates their importance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Argentina shipped forty-seven tons to Japan in July, after much larger prewar exports, but its total available supply remained small. Japan might turn to Argentina because Mexican material was unavailable, yet estimated Argentine output was far below the roughly 7,000 tons needed annually for maximum Japanese synthetic-cryolite production. Reid-Adam therefore regarded the trade as worth noting but not alarming.

subfiles.title: File charge slip for 894.24
subfiles.about: The slip records the temporary charging or circulation of material from file 894.24.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten names, dates, and enclosure references document movement of file material. Much of the writing is illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Notice of omitted file numbers
subfiles.about: The note states that file items 894.24/1628 through 894.24/1727 were omitted.
subfiles.summary: This is a brief records-management notice. It marks a numerical gap in the sequence of documents.

subfiles.title: Second file charge slip
subfiles.about: A second charge slip records circulation of an enclosure or file item.
subfiles.summary: Only fragmentary handwritten entries and a Government Printing Office form number are legible. The specific borrower and enclosure cannot be confidently identified.

subfiles.title: Commercial Affairs note identifying Beltramo firms
subfiles.about: The note comments on records concerning Beltramo and related firms in São Paulo.
subfiles.summary: It appears to say that Beltramo Filhos succeeded Beltramo e Cia. in São Paulo in 1936. The remainder discusses what can be inferred about the name or business, but the handwriting and OCR are too damaged for certainty.

subfiles.title: Assistant Secretary routing note on an attachment
subfiles.from: Office of an Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The writer forwards an attachment believed likely to interest another official.
subfiles.summary: The short handwritten note asks that the attached material be passed along. Names and the precise wording are largely illegible.

subfiles.title: Mitsui offers of Brazilian graphite, rutile, tantalite, and zircon
subfiles.about: Reid-Adam reports secret intelligence on large mineral offers submitted by Mitsui's São Paulo office for possible shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The offers covered graphite, rutile, tantalite, and zircon, with some quantities proposed on a recurring monthly basis. Reid-Adam suggests that rutile and zircon transactions might be attempts to circumvent the U.S.-Brazilian agreement and questions whether the claimed graphite could be Mexican material routed through Brazil or the United States. He also stresses the military-industrial value of tantalite and notes that Brazil had exported 17.2 tons to Japan during January-August 1941.

subfiles.title: Inquiry concerning addition to the Proclaimed List
subfiles.about: Dickey reports an inquiry to the U.S. Embassy in Mexico City about possible additions to the Proclaimed List.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy was being asked for information about the unidentified persons or firms under consideration. The results would be used to decide whether they should be placed on the Proclaimed List.

subfiles.title: Routing query concerning instructions and telegram paraphrases
subfiles.about: The note asks whether instructions should be sent to the embassy and mentions Dickey's paraphrases of three telegrams.
subfiles.summary: The handwriting appears to raise a question about further guidance to the embassy. It also notes that Dickey should have paraphrases of three related telegrams.

subfiles.title: Manzanillo warning of concealed mercury aboard Azuma Maru
subfiles.about: Hoyt reports an urgent effort to stop mercury concealed in other export goods from being loaded aboard the Japanese vessel Azuma Maru.
subfiles.summary: Acting on reliable information, Hoyt and the British vice consul warned the local customs chief that mercury might be hidden in boxes of resin or other cargo. Bronze pieces in metal containers were already being loaded, so customs halted exports until the containers and resin boxes could be inspected. Hoyt states that the consular office had positive proof that such a smuggling plan had been contemplated.

subfiles.title: Discovery and embargo of concealed mercury at Manzanillo
subfiles.about: A follow-up telegram reports that mercury was found in drums declared to contain bronze and that the entire shipment was embargoed.
subfiles.summary: Five mercury flasks were found in the first opened drum, and officials believed all 347 drums contained mercury. The shipment was attributed to local customs broker Antonio Llorens, while the Mexico City agent was thought to be a Japanese man named Nagabuchi at Bucareli 8. Customs authorities were opening the remaining containers.
